confirmed.file: contracts/src/VenmoToSepaRouter.sol:268-313 (and the absence of any offRamp.cancelIntent call)
confirmed.evidence: cancel() and rescueTimedOut() both gate on `if (transfer.status != TransferStatus.PENDING) revert TransferNotPending();` (lines 273 and 296). commit() sets `transfer.status = TransferStatus.COMMITTED` and moves the USDC into OffRampV3 via offRamp.selectQuoteAndCommit (router is the OffRampV3 depositor). grep confirms the router only ever calls offRamp.createIntent, offRamp.selectQuoteAndCommit, offRamp.getIntent — it NEVER calls offRamp.cancelIntent. OffRampV3.cancelIntent requires `msg.sender == depositor` (line 298), i.e. the router, after committedAt + FULFILLMENT_WINDOW.
confirmed.why: After a user commits and the selected solver never fulfills, the user's USDC is in OffRampV3 with the router as depositor. There is no router-callable path to invoke OffRampV3.cancelIntent, and the router's own cancel()/rescueTimedOut() revert once status is COMMITTED. The funds are permanently locked except via owner-only emergencyWithdraw (and OffRampV3.emergencyWithdraw at that — VenmoToSepaRouter.emergencyWithdraw can't touch funds that sit inside OffRampV3). A solver no-show after commit therefore strands user principal with no trustless recovery.
confirmed.fix: Add a permissionless router function, e.g. rescueCommitted(address user), that: checks status == COMMITTED and block.timestamp > intent.committedAt + offRamp.FULFILLMENT_WINDOW, calls offRamp.cancelIntent(transfer.intentId) (which returns USDC to the router as depositor), then usdc.safeTransfer(user, transfer.usdcAmount) and sets status = EXPIRED.

confirmed.evidence: The duplicate-transfer guard only blocks PENDING: `if (pendingTransfers[user].status == TransferStatus.PENDING) { revert UserAlreadyHasPendingTransfer(); }`. For any other status (COMMITTED, COMPLETED, CANCELLED, EXPIRED) execute() proceeds and unconditionally overwrites `pendingTransfers[user] = PendingTransfer({...})` at lines 194-203.
confirmed.why: If a user initiates a second ZKP2P Venmo onramp while their first transfer is still COMMITTED (USDC in OffRampV3, solver about to send EUR), execute() overwrites pendingTransfers[user] with the new intent. The first transfer's router-side record is destroyed: markComplete(user) can no longer be called for it (it now reads the new intent), and the COMMITTED-rescue path proposed above keys off the same single mapping slot, so the first intent becomes permanently unaddressable from the router. Combined with finding #1, this turns a recoverable lock into an unrecoverable one. One-pending-transfer-per-user is the contract's core invariant and it is not enforced across the COMMITTED state.
confirmed.fix: Tighten the guard to block any active transfer: `if (pendingTransfers[user].status == TransferStatus.PENDING || pendingTransfers[user].status == TransferStatus.COMMITTED) revert UserAlreadyHasPendingTransfer();` (or maintain per-intent records keyed by intentId instead of one slot per user).

confirmed.evidence: commit(address solver, uint256 quotedEurAmount) checks slippage as `if (quotedEurAmount < transfer.minEurAmount) revert SlippageExceeded(quotedEurAmount, transfer.minEurAmount);`. quotedEurAmount is a caller-supplied argument; it is never cross-checked against the actual on-chain quote. The router does not read quotes[intentId][solver][SEPA_INSTANT].fiatAmount before committing — it passes solver straight to offRamp.selectQuoteAndCommit, which sets intent.selectedFiatAmount = quote.fiatAmount from on-chain state independently of quotedEurAmount.
confirmed.why: The slippage guard binds to nothing real. The value the user is actually protected against is selectedFiatAmount (the solver's on-chain quote), and the downstream OffRampV3 fulfillment only requires the solver to send >= 99% of that. A caller can pass quotedEurAmount == minEurAmount while selecting a solver whose true on-chain quote is far lower, so the guard provides false assurance. The frontend likely auto-fills quotedEurAmount from the displayed quote, so a solver that posts a low on-chain quote (different from what the UI fetched) can have the user commit below their intended floor. SlippageExceeded should compare against the binding on-chain quote, not a free parameter.
confirmed.fix: Read the real quote inside commit() and validate against it: `OffRampV3.Quote memory q = offRamp.getQuote(transfer.intentId, solver, OffRampV3.RTPN.SEPA_INSTANT); if (q.fiatAmount < transfer.minEurAmount) revert SlippageExceeded(q.fiatAmount, transfer.minEurAmount);` and drop the quotedEurAmount parameter (or keep it only as a UI echo, never as the checked value).

confirmed.evidence: `if (attestation.amount < intent.selectedFiatAmount * 99 / 100) revert AmountMismatch();` — attestation.amount is the EUR the solver actually sent (TLSNotary-proven, cents) and selectedFiatAmount is the EUR the user was promised by the selected quote (cents). The check accepts any payment >= 99% of the promised amount.
confirmed.why: A solver can under-pay the user by up to 1% of the committed fiat amount and still claim 100% of the escrowed USDC. The comment calls this 'tolerance for rounding', but 1% is far larger than rounding on a 2-decimal (cents) figure — on a EUR 1,000 transfer the solver may legally short the recipient by EUR 10. Since the solver is UNTRUSTED and chooses how much fiat to send, this is a systematic value-extraction allowance, not rounding.
confirmed.fix: Drop the tolerance to a rounding-scale epsilon or remove it: e.g. `if (attestation.amount + 1 < intent.selectedFiatAmount) revert AmountMismatch();` (allow at most 1 cent under) — the solver can always send slightly more without penalty since there is no upper bound.

confirmed.evidence: verifyPayment consumes the nullifier (usedNullifiers[nullifier] = true at line 107) on the FIRST successful signature+witness check, independent of intent state. In OffRampV3.fulfillIntentWithProof the amount check (line 386, reverts AmountMismatch) runs BEFORE verifier.verifyPayment (line 389), so a wrong-amount attempt does not burn the nullifier — good. However OffRampV3 also derives its own transferId = keccak256(attestation.paymentId) and checks usedTransferIds AFTER calling verifyPayment (lines 393-394), so the PaymentVerifier nullifier and the OffRampV3 usedTransferIds are two independent single-use stores keyed on the same paymentId.
confirmed.why: Double nullifier bookkeeping (verifier.usedNullifiers and offRamp.usedTransferIds) over the same paymentId is redundant and creates a subtle ordering hazard: if any future caller invokes verifier.verifyPayment for an intent (e.g. via a different consumer) the nullifier burns there, but OffRampV3.usedTransferIds is only set inside fulfillIntentWithProof. The current single-consumer flow is safe, but the redundancy is dead-weight state and an easy source of future replay-logic confusion. Not exploitable today.
confirmed.fix: Pick one nullifier store. Since verifyPayment already enforces single-use on paymentId, remove OffRampV3's separate usedTransferIds gate (or make OffRampV3 rely solely on the verifier's NullifierAlreadyUsed revert) to keep a single source of truth.

confirmed.evidence: validate_payment compares the proven IBAN ONLY against the solver-supplied request field: `let expected_iban = normalize_iban(&request.expected_beneficiary_iban); ... if expected_iban != actual_iban { return Err(...) }`. `expected_beneficiary_iban` comes from the untrusted solver's POST body (attestation.rs:22). chain.rs::OnChainIntent decodes only depositor/usdcAmount/status/selectedSolver/selectedFiatAmount and explicitly skips the dynamic strings; it NEVER reads the on-chain `Intent.receivingInfo` (the user's real IBAN, OffRampV3.sol:93). validate_intent (chain.rs:234) therefore never compares the proven IBAN to the chain. OffRampV3.fulfillIntentWithProof (OffRampV3.sol:367-409) checks only intentHash and `attestation.amount` vs selectedFiatAmount; the IBAN lives inside the opaque `dataHash` and is unchecked on-chain.
confirmed.why: The attestation service is the TRUSTED component and the ONLY place the paid IBAN can be bound to the user's intended recipient (on-chain dataHash is opaque). Under the documented trust model (solver = UNTRUSTED, OffRampV3 = permissionless 'anyone can fulfill'), a malicious/compromised solver sends EUR to an IBAN it controls, generates a valid TLSNotary proof of that payment, sets expected_beneficiary_iban to the SAME attacker IBAN, obtains the witness signature, and calls fulfillIntentWithProof to claim the user's USDC. The user surrenders USDC and never receives EUR. Direct fund loss; the witness signature is the authorization that releases custody.
confirmed.fix: Bind the IBAN to chain, not to solver input. In chain.rs decode the dynamic `receivingInfo` string from the getIntent tuple (follow its offset word in the tail), expose it on OnChainIntent, and in validate_intent require normalize_iban(proven_iban) == normalize_iban(onchain_receivingInfo). Ignore request.expected_beneficiary_iban for authorization (or assert it equals the chain value). Pass the VerifiedPayment IBAN into validate_intent so the check happens before signing.

confirmed.file: attestation/src/attestation.rs:102-142 (validate_payment) and create_attestation:73-79 — verified.status is never checked
confirmed.evidence: verification.rs parses the transfer/transaction `status` into VerifiedPayment.status (verification.rs:81,209-213), and present_transfer.rs:3 reveals it in the transcript, but grep confirms NO check of status in validate_payment, validate_intent, or create_attestation (only on-chain IntentStatus is checked). Qonto transfer status is one of pending|processing|canceled|declined|settled (solver/src/providers/qonto-types.ts:101-106); only `settled` means funds moved, and declined_reason includes debit_account_insufficient_funds.
confirmed.why: On-chain cannot see the payment status (dataHash is opaque), so the witness is the only enforcer. The honest prover queries `status=completed` (providers/.../prove_transfer.rs:68), but the prover runs on the UNTRUSTED solver's machine and can prove a transfer in ANY status. A solver proves a `declined`/`canceled`/`pending` transfer whose amount+IBAN match, gets the witness signature, and claims USDC for a payment that never settled (or was reversed). Fund loss for the user.
confirmed.fix: In validate_payment require the proven status to be a terminal success value, e.g. `match verified.status.as_deref() { Some("settled") | Some("completed") => {}, other => return Err(InvalidPaymentData(...)) }`, and reject when status is missing.

confirmed.why: A production 'for testing' bypass: by sending expected_amount_cents=0 and empty expected_beneficiary_iban, an untrusted solver disables BOTH the off-chain amount and IBAN validations in one shot. The on-chain `attestation.amount >= selectedFiatAmount*99/100` still constrains amount (because create_attestation always signs the real proven amount), but IBAN remains entirely unbound — compounding the Critical IBAN finding and removing the service's defense-in-depth.
confirmed.fix: Delete the skip branch. Make validation unconditional and instead derive the expected amount/IBAN from the on-chain intent (see IBAN fix), never from solver-supplied fields. If a test mode is required, gate it behind a compile-time cfg(test) or an explicit, off-by-default env flag — never on request content.

confirmed.evidence: `amount: verified.amount_cents.unwrap_or(0) as u64,` where amount_cents is i64. A negative value casts to a huge u64 (e.g. -5000 -> 18446744073709546616) which becomes the SIGNED attestation.amount. validate_payment only rejects on `actual != expected` (exact match), and if the solver sets a negative expected_amount_cents, chain.rs:282 `expected_amount_cents > 0` is false so the on-chain amount-vs-chain comparison is skipped; the signed huge amount then satisfies OffRampV3's `attestation.amount >= selectedFiatAmount*99/100`.
confirmed.why: Defense-in-depth gap: an unvalidated signed i64->u64 cast lets a negative proven amount become an enormous positive on-chain amount and side-steps the min-amount guard. Tagged SUSPECT because Qonto outbound transfers report positive amount_cents (qonto-types.ts:141), so live exploitation depends on the proven JSON carrying a negative amount (e.g. a debit-side transaction). The unsound cast is real regardless.
confirmed.fix: Reject negative/None amounts before signing: require `let amount = verified.amount_cents.filter(|&c| c > 0).ok_or(MissingField("amount_cents"))? as u64;` and reject any request with expected_amount_cents <= 0 in validate_intent rather than skipping the check.

confirmed.evidence: extract_amount uses `regex::Regex::new(r"(\d+)\.?(\d{0,2})")` with `.find()` (first match). Verified empirically against redacted Qonto JSON: it returns the first digit-run anywhere — e.g. a UUID fragment `019` or a date `2026` — not the payment amount. This fallback is reachable: extract_json_body returns a `{...}` slice that fails serde_json parse whenever selective disclosure redacts bytes inside the JSON (verification.rs:218 falls through to regex). extract_iban similarly takes the first IBAN-shaped substring, not necessarily the counterparty's.
confirmed.why: When the proof uses selective disclosure that breaks JSON validity, the amount/IBAN the witness signs are derived by grabbing the first matching substring, which is almost never the true field. Today the exact-match amount check and on-chain min-amount guard mostly mask this (it causes false rejections / DoS of legitimate proofs), but it is brittle and becomes a fund-loss vector the moment those guards are relaxed or the IBAN check is fixed to rely on this value.
confirmed.fix: Drop the heuristic regex fallback. Require a successfully-parsed JSON object with explicit, keyed fields (transfer.amount_cents, counterparty IBAN, status); if the disclosed transcript is not valid keyed JSON, reject the attestation rather than guessing.

confirmed.file: attestation/src/verification.rs:60-65 (server allowlist) and 67-92 (request path never inspected)
confirmed.evidence: Host allowlist is a substring match: `if !allowed_servers.iter().any(|s| server_name.contains(s))`. The code only parses `partial_transcript.received_unsafe()` (the response); it never inspects the sent request line, so it does not verify the proof targeted the `/v2/transactions` endpoint vs any other path on the allowed host.
confirmed.why: substring matching is loose (a SNI like `thirdparty.qonto.com.evil.tld` contains the allowed string), though this is gated by TLS cert validation under default root CAs so it is not directly exploitable. Not checking the request path means the witness trusts that any 200 body on the host is a transaction query; combined with the lenient body parser this widens what an attacker-shaped response can look like.
confirmed.fix: Use exact/suffix host matching (e.g. server_name == s || server_name.ends_with(&format!(".{}", s))) and assert the sent transcript's request target starts with the expected `/v2/transactions` path before extracting payment data.

confirmed.evidence: PaymentVerifier declares `error TimestampTooOld();` (line 59) but it is never used; there is no timestamp/freshness check in verifyPayment. The attestation service signs `timestamp: connection_info.time` (the TLS session time) without any staleness bound. EIP-712 domain and struct hashing are byte-identical between Rust (eip712.rs:49-99) and Solidity (PaymentVerifier.sol:65-75,161-170) — that parity is correct.
confirmed.why: There is no proof-expiry enforced by the witness or the verifier; an attestation is only time-bounded by OffRampV3.FULFILLMENT_WINDOW and by nullifier single-use. Low severity because those two mechanisms prevent replay and stale fulfillment, but the unused error and absent freshness check are latent (and misleading) — a stale proof for a long-lived intent could still be signed.
confirmed.fix: Either remove the unused TimestampTooOld error, or enforce freshness: reject in validate_intent when verified.timestamp is older than a configured max age (and/or have the contract revert on stale attestation.timestamp). Document that fulfillment-window + nullifier are the intended bounds if no change is made.

The `/api/quote` route's Quote interface (frontend/app/api/quote/route.ts:17-27) defines `fiatAmount: number` and has NO `outputAmount` field; the solver emits `fiatAmount` everywhere and `outputAmount` appears nowhere in solver/* (grep confirmed 0 hits). So `best.outputAmount` is `undefined`, making `quotedEurAmount` undefined. Then handleRouterCommit (line 842) does `BigInt(Math.floor(flowData.quotedEurAmount * 100))` = `BigInt(Math.floor(NaN))` = `BigInt(NaN)`, which throws `RangeError: NaN cannot be converted to a BigInt`. The user may commit to a worse rate than they reviewed, with no client-side minimum-output check. Severity is bounded because the solver fulfills with the committed on-chain `selectedFiatAmount` (solver/src/orchestrator-v3.ts:493,507,649) which the contract should enforce as a floor — so this is a 'pay less than displayed' risk, not direct theft. confirmed.evidence: `function commit(address solver, uint256 quotedEurAmount)` then `if (quotedEurAmount < transfer.minEurAmount) { revert SlippageExceeded(quotedEurAmount, transfer.minEurAmount); }`. `quotedEurAmount` is a caller-supplied parameter; it is NEVER read from the on-chain quote. The subsequent `offRamp.selectQuoteAndCommit(transfer.intentId, solver, RTPN.SEPA_INSTANT, transfer.iban, transfer.recipientName)` does not take or check an EUR amount — OffRampV3 independently reads `quote.fiatAmount` from storage (OffRampV3.sol:283).
confirmed.why: The 'slippage protection' compares the user's own minEur against a number the same user passes in — it binds nothing about the actual solver quote. It reads as a security guard (named SlippageExceeded, documented as 'slippage check') but provides zero protection against a low-paying quote. Real binding happens elsewhere: the user chooses `solver` (a specific quote viewed off-chain) and OffRampV3.fulfillIntentWithProof:386 enforces `attestation.amount >= selectedFiatAmount*99/100` against the real quote. So the guard is misleading dead logic, not an exploitable hole (caller == beneficiary).
confirmed.fix: Either read the real quote on-chain (`offRamp.getQuote(transfer.intentId, solver, RTPN.SEPA_INSTANT).fiatAmount`) and compare that to `minEurAmount`, or drop the `quotedEurAmount` param and the check entirely and rely on OffRampV3's fulfillment amount enforcement.

confirmed.evidence: `if (pendingTransfers[user].status == TransferStatus.PENDING) { revert UserAlreadyHasPendingTransfer(); }` ... `pendingTransfers[user] = PendingTransfer({...status: TransferStatus.PENDING});`. The duplicate guard only blocks status==PENDING. `pendingTransfers` is a single slot per user. If a user's prior transfer is COMMITTED (USDC already forwarded to OffRampV3, intent1 awaiting solver) or COMPLETED/CANCELLED/EXPIRED, a second onramp passes the guard and OVERWRITES the struct (new intentId/usdcAmount), pulling a second `executableAmount` into the router.
confirmed.why: The first intent's USDC is safe — it lives in OffRampV3 keyed by intent1 (depositor=router) and the solver still fulfills it there, paying USDC to the solver and EUR to the user. But the router loses its reference to intent1: `markComplete(user)` (line 319-336) can now only ever inspect intent2, so the first transfer can never be marked COMPLETED. No direct theft, but it is an orphaned-state / accounting bug that breaks the router's status bookkeeping and could confuse off-chain monitoring or any future logic that trusts router status.
confirmed.fix: Block re-execute unless the slot is cleared: `if (pendingTransfers[user].status != TransferStatus.NONE && pendingTransfers[user].status != TransferStatus.COMPLETED && pendingTransfers[user].status != TransferStatus.CANCELLED && pendingTransfers[user].status != TransferStatus.EXPIRED) revert UserAlreadyHasPendingTransfer();` (i.e., reject while PENDING or COMMITTED).

confirmed.evidence: `if request.expected_amount_cents == 0 && request.expected_beneficiary_iban.is_empty() { return Ok(()); }` — when the caller (solver, UNTRUSTED) supplies zero amount and empty IBAN, the attestation service skips BOTH the amount and beneficiary-IBAN checks and signs whatever the TLS proof contains.

confirmed.evidence: function commit(address solver, uint256 quotedEurAmount) ... if (quotedEurAmount < transfer.minEurAmount) revert SlippageExceeded(quotedEurAmount, transfer.minEurAmount); ... offRamp.selectQuoteAndCommit(transfer.intentId, solver, OffRampV3.RTPN.SEPA_INSTANT, transfer.iban, transfer.recipientName);
confirmed.why: The slippage floor (minEurAmount, the user's protection carried from the Venmo step) is enforced against quotedEurAmount, which is a caller-supplied parameter. The router never reads the actual on-chain quote (grep confirms no getQuote / quotes[ access in the contract). selectQuoteAndCommit independently reads quotes[intentId][solver][SEPA_INSTANT].fiatAmount and stores it as selectedFiatAmount (OffRampV3.sol:283); that on-chain value — not quotedEurAmount — is what fulfillIntentWithProof binds settlement to (attestation.amount >= selectedFiatAmount*99/100, OffRampV3.sol:386). There is no link between the asserted quotedEurAmount and the committed quote, so the slippage check is non-binding: committing to a solver whose real on-chain fiatAmount is below minEurAmount passes the guard, and the user receives less EUR than their stated minimum. A buggy or hostile frontend supplies quotedEurAmount=minEurAmount regardless of the real quote.
confirmed.fix: Read and validate the real quote inside commit(): OffRampV3.Quote memory q = offRamp.getQuote(transfer.intentId, solver, OffRampV3.RTPN.SEPA_INSTANT); if (q.fiatAmount < transfer.minEurAmount) revert SlippageExceeded(q.fiatAmount, transfer.minEurAmount); and drop the untrusted quotedEurAmount parameter.

confirmed.evidence: const authorized = await this.chain.isAuthorizedSolver(); if (!authorized) { ... throw new Error("Solver not authorized"); }  — isAuthorizedSolver() (client-v3.ts:81-91) returns solverSupportsRtpn(solver, SEPA_INSTANT). submitQuotesForIntent also gates on it: "const authorized = await this.chain.solverSupportsRtpn(rtpn); if (!authorized) { ... continue; }" (lines 306-313).
confirmed.why: OffRampV3 is explicitly permissionless (contract comment line 13: "V3 removes authorized solver requirement"). solverSupportsRtpn is an OPTIONAL self-set reputation mapping that defaults to false and is only set by the solver calling setSolverRtpn (OffRampV3.sol:490). A freshly deployed solver that has not called setSolverRtpn will (a) throw "Solver not authorized" at startup and refuse to run, and (b) even if it bypassed startup, skip quoting for every RTPN. This is a self-imposed gate the contract does not require; it makes the solver non-functional out of the box and the misleading name/log ("Solver is not authorized on the contract!") will send ops down the wrong path. Marked M/SUSPECT-confidence because it may be an intentional opt-in convention, but it contradicts the permissionless design and the throw blocks startup.
confirmed.fix: Either remove the isAuthorizedSolver() startup throw and the per-RTPN solverSupportsRtpn gate (rely on provider registry for capability), or ensure deployment runbook calls setSolverRtpn for each supported RTPN and rename the check/log to reflect it is an optional reputation flag, not authorization.

confirmed.evidence: encodeHookPayload uses the FLAT form: `encodeAbiParameters(parseAbiParameters("string, string, uint256"), [iban, recipientName, minEurAmount])`. I proved with viem itself that the flat encoding's first word is 0x60 / 224 bytes, while the struct/tuple encoding's first word is 0x20 / 256 bytes — they are NOT equal. I proved in Foundry that decoding the flat encoding as the struct REVERTS (memory panic 0x41 / expectRevert PASS). The 25 existing router tests pass only because the test helper `_encodePayload` (VenmoToSepaRouter.t.sol:110) uses the correct struct form `abi.encode(HookPayload({...}))`, so production encoding is never exercised.
confirmed.why: VenmoToSepaRouter.execute() runs synchronously inside ZKP2P OrchestratorV2.fulfillIntent (hooks are called directly; AcrossBridgeHookV2 is the canonical pull-model example and there is no try/catch around post-intent hooks — the propagation step is the one inferred link). When the user's Venmo proof triggers fulfillIntent, execute() reverts in abi.decode, so fulfillIntent reverts. The entire Venmo->SEPA happy path can never complete: the ZKP2P onramp intent never releases USDC to the router, yet the user already made the off-chain Venmo payment. confirmed.evidence: commit() takes `uint256 quotedEurAmount` from the caller and checks slippage ONLY against that argument: line 234 `if (quotedEurAmount < transfer.minEurAmount) revert SlippageExceeded(...)`. The value that actually binds the solver is the on-chain `quote.fiatAmount` set in OffRampV3.submitQuote and copied into `intent.selectedFiatAmount` by selectQuoteAndCommit (OffRampV3.sol:283) — which never compares against minEurAmount. The frontend passes `best.outputAmount` from the off-chain FreeFlo quote API (VenmoToSepaFlow.tsx:821,842), NOT the on-chain quote, so there is no on-chain link between the checked value and the committed value. I wrote and ran a Foundry PoC: user floor = 8500 cents; malicious solver submits an on-chain quote of 1000 cents; user calls commit(SOLVER, 8500); commit SUCCEEDS and the intent is COMMITTED at selectedFiatAmount = 1000 (8.5x below the floor) with 100 USDC locked to that solver. Test passed.
confirmed.why: The protocol's trust model is explicit that the solver is UNTRUSTED and permissionless (any address can quote/fulfill). The minEurAmount slippage guard is the user's only on-chain protection on the offramp leg, and it is decorative: it constrains a caller-supplied number, not the untrusted solver's on-chain quote. A malicious/buggy solver advertises a good rate off-chain (passing the floor) but commits a far lower on-chain quote; downstream fulfillIntentWithProof only requires the solver to send that low committed amount (OffRampV3.sol:386 `attestation.amount >= selectedFiatAmount*99/100`). Net: user pays full USDC, receives far less EUR than their stated minimum. Direct, silent loss of user funds.
confirmed.fix: Drop the `quotedEurAmount` parameter and read the binding quote on-chain inside commit(): `OffRampV3.Quote memory q = offRamp.getQuote(transfer.intentId, solver, OffRampV3.RTPN.SEPA_INSTANT); if (q.fiatAmount < transfer.minEurAmount) revert SlippageExceeded(q.fiatAmount, transfer.minEurAmount);`. This makes the floor enforce against the value that actually settles.

confirmed.evidence: execute() validates IBAN/recipientName only for non-empty (lines 173-175 `bytes(payload.iban).length == 0 || bytes(payload.recipientName).length == 0`). It stores them and creates the FreeFlo intent (locking USDC into the router) BEFORE any length cap. But OffRampV3.selectQuoteAndCommit enforces `receivingInfo.length <= 256` and `recipientName.length <= 70` (OffRampV3.sol:259-264). So a payload with recipientName > 70 chars (or IBAN > 256) passes execute() but makes every later commit() revert with InvalidRecipientName/InvalidReceivingInfo.
confirmed.why: Self-inflicted by the user, and recoverable: USDC is returned via cancel() or rescueTimedOut() after the 30-min COMMIT_TIMEOUT. But it traps funds for 30 minutes with a confusing failure and no early signal. Defense-in-depth gap at the trust boundary where untrusted signalHookData first enters.
confirmed.fix: Validate the same length bounds in execute() before creating the intent: `if (bytes(payload.iban).length > 256 || bytes(payload.recipientName).length > 70) revert InvalidPayload();` so bad payloads fail fast without locking funds.

confirmed.evidence: The duplicate-transfer guard only blocks status == PENDING: line 165 `if (pendingTransfers[user].status == TransferStatus.PENDING) revert UserAlreadyHasPendingTransfer();`. If the user already has a COMMITTED (in-flight) transfer and completes a second ZKP2P onramp, execute() overwrites pendingTransfers[user] (line 194) with the new transfer, discarding the old intentId. The old FreeFlo intent still exists and settles independently on OffRampV3 (USDC already moved there), but the router can no longer markComplete the old one.

The overwrite of a live COMMITTED record is nonetheless a state-tracking inconsistency that could confuse the UI/ops and orphan the old transfer's status. Requires two concurrent onramps, so low likelihood.
confirmed.fix: Block overwrite for any non-terminal state, e.g. `if (pendingTransfers[user].status == TransferStatus.PENDING || pendingTransfers[user].status == TransferStatus.COMMITTED) revert UserAlreadyHasPendingTransfer();`.

[CRITICAL — VERIFIED] The prover is its own notary using a hardcoded DUMMY key, which collapses the TLSNotary trust model. A malicious/compromised solver can forge payment proofs and claim USDC without sending fiat.
- File: providers/prover/adapters/qonto/src/prove_transfer.rs:379-383
  // Load signing key (dummy for local testing)
  let signing_key = k256::ecdsa::SigningKey::from_bytes(&[1u8; 32].into())?;
  let signer = Box::new(Secp256k1Signer::new(&signing_key.to_bytes())?);
  let mut provider = CryptoProvider::default();
  provider.signer.set_signer(signer);
- The "notary" runs IN-PROCESS, in the SAME binary the solver executes: prove_transfer.rs:87 `tokio::spawn(async move { notary(notary_socket, request_rx, attestation_tx).await.unwrap() });` — prover and notary share one process via tokio::io::duplex (line 82). There is no independent/remote notary.
- Why this is fatal to the money path: the project's own .claude/rules/security-invariants.md states "Solver: UNTRUSTED. Cannot forge proofs." In real TLSNotary the notary MUST be a separate trusted party so an untrusted prover cannot fabricate the transcript. Here the solver controls both sides AND signs the attestation with a publicly-known key ([1u8;32]). The solver can therefore hand-craft any transcript (arbitrary amount_cents, beneficiary IBAN, transaction id, status="completed") and self-notarize it.
- Confirmed it is consumed downstream, not dead test code: solver/src/attestation/prover.ts:56-97 spawns `qonto_prove_transfer` then `qonto_present_transfer` and base64-encodes qonto_transfer.presentation.tlsn for the attestation service. The attestation service then verifies with attestation/src/verification.rs:42-52 `let crypto_provider = CryptoProvider::default(); ... presentation.verify(&crypto_provider)` and NO notary verifying-key is pinned anywhere (grep of attestation/src/config.rs + env examples: zero NOTARY / trusted-key references). So the service accepts whatever notary key is embedded — i.e. the solver's dummy key — then signs an EIP-712 PaymentAttestation. attestation/src/attestation.rs:84-85 signs with the real witness key. End-to-end: untrusted solver -> forged self-notarized transcript -> signed witness attestation -> USDC release.
- Aggravating: attestation/src/attestation.rs validate_payment() cross-checks only against request.expected_amount_cents / expected_beneficiary_iban, which come from the SAME untrusted request body (not on-chain), and it short-circuits to Ok(()) when those are 0/empty (attestation.rs ~line 110: "If expected values are 0/empty, skip validation (for testing)"). So there is no independent mitigation.
- Smallest fix (prover side, within this component): do NOT self-notarize. Replace the in-process notary with a connection to a real, FreeFlo-controlled remote Notary server whose verifying key is known in advance; remove the hardcoded [1u8;32] signer entirely. Correspondingly the attestation service MUST pin that notary's verifying key in presentation.verify (configure CryptoProvider with the trusted notary key instead of default()). Both halves are required — fixing only one leaves the hole open.
- Scope/ASK: I cannot see the production deployment, so it's possible a real remote notary is wired elsewhere and these two binaries are a stale local-dev harness. But as committed and as invoked by solver/src/attestation/prover.ts, this IS the path. Needs human confirmation of intent (ASK) before it's considered anything other than exploitable.

(line 74, with honest inline comment "reveal the full JSON body"), yet lines 87-91 then print "Redacted fields: settled_balance / bank_account_id / initiator_id" which are NOT redacted when they appear in the same transaction object. Only the Authorization request header is actually withheld (lines 40-51, correct). This is a correctness/clarity issue, not a fund-loss issue (account balance / internal IDs leak to the attestation service, which is already TRUSTED).
